title: Experiments, correlations and sampling
summary: Types of experiment, variables, designs and hypotheses, correlational studies, and how samples are chosen.

keyterms.definition: The variable the researcher manipulates to see its effect.
The variable that is measured to see whether the IV had an effect.
A precise, testable prediction of the relationship between variables.
An experiment in a controlled setting where the IV is manipulated; high control, often lower ecological validity.
An experiment in a natural setting where the IV is still manipulated by the researcher.
Compares groups that differ on a pre-existing characteristic (e.g. gender, age), so there is no random allocation.
The IV varies naturally (e.g. a policy change) and the researcher measures its effect.
Different participants take part in each condition.
The same participants take part in all conditions; counterbalancing controls order effects.
Every member of the target population has an equal chance of selection.
Selecting people who are available and willing at the time.
Participants volunteer, e.g. by answering an advert.
How far findings from a sample can be applied to the wider population.

questions.prompt: A researcher compares memory in people aged 20 and 70. What type of study is this?
questions.explanation: Age cannot be randomly assigned, so this is a quasi-experiment and causal claims are weaker.

questions.prompt: Which design has no participant variables between conditions but risks order effects?
questions.explanation: The same people do both conditions; counterbalancing reduces practice and fatigue effects.

questions.statement: In a field experiment the researcher still manipulates the IV.
questions.explanation: The setting is natural but the IV is controlled by the researcher, unlike a natural experiment.

questions.statement: The dependent variable is the one the researcher manipulates.
questions.explanation: The IV is manipulated; the DV is measured.

questions.text: Participants who cannot be randomly allocated to groups because they differ on a pre-existing trait are studied in a ___-experiment.
questions.explanation: Quasi-experiments use naturally occurring groups.

questions.text: "Participants who hear words in a quiet room will recall more words than those in a noisy room" is a ___ hypothesis.
questions.explanation: It predicts the direction of the difference.

questions.prompt: Match each study to its experiment type.

pairs.left: Loftus & Palmer (1974): verb wording in lab
Researchers vary a shop sign and record purchases
Comparing children before and after TV arrived in a town

questions.explanation: The key questions: who controls the IV, and is allocation random?

questions.prompt: Why do researchers counterbalance in a repeated measures design?
questions.explanation: Half the participants do A then B, half B then A, so order effects cancel out.

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest advantage of a lab experiment?
questions.explanation: Control allows cause-and-effect conclusions (internal validity).

questions.prompt: Order the steps of planning an experiment.
questions.explanation: Variables must be defined before a precise hypothesis can be written.

questions.prompt: Which sampling technique gives every member of the target population an equal chance of selection?
questions.explanation: Random sampling reduces sampling bias, though it is hard to achieve in practice.

questions.prompt: A researcher puts up a poster asking for volunteers. What is the main risk?
options: Volunteers may differ from the population (e.g. more motivated)
questions.explanation: Self-selected samples may be biased, limiting generalizability.

questions.statement: Opportunity sampling is quick and easy but often unrepresentative.
questions.explanation: Choosing whoever is available, e.g. students, can bias the sample.

questions.statement: A correlational study manipulates an independent variable.
questions.explanation: Correlational studies measure two co-variables without manipulation.

questions.text: How far results from a sample apply to the wider population is called ___.
questions.explanation: Representative sampling improves generalizability.

questions.text: In a correlation, the variables are called co-___.
questions.explanation: Neither is an IV or DV; both are measured.

questions.prompt: Match each sampling technique to a description.

pairs.right: Names drawn from the full list
Students in the canteen at lunch
People replying to an online advert

questions.explanation: Snowball sampling is useful for hard-to-reach groups.

questions.prompt: A scatter graph shows points rising from bottom-left to top-right. This shows:
questions.explanation: As one variable increases, so does the other.

questions.prompt: Why might a researcher choose a correlational study instead of an experiment?
options: Because manipulating the variable (e.g. childhood trauma) would be unethical
questions.explanation: Correlational studies can examine variables that cannot ethically be manipulated.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of drawing a random sample.
items: Obtain a list of all members
Use a random number generator to select
questions.explanation: A complete list (sampling frame) is required.
